title: Strong convergence of an inertial Tseng's extragradient algorithm for pseudomonotone variational inequalities with applications to optimal control problems
problem: How can a variational inequality driven by a pseudomonotone, Lipschitz operator be solved iteratively with strong (norm) convergence in a Hilbert space, without knowing the operator's Lipschitz constant in advance and without computing more than one projection onto the feasible set per iteration?
setting: A real Hilbert space with a nonempty closed convex feasible set; the governing operator is pseudomonotone (weaker than monotone), Lipschitz continuous, and sequentially weakly continuous, with a nonempty solution set. Infinite-dimensional setting, deterministic iteration, asymptotic analysis; numerical tests include a variational inequality arising from an optimal control problem.
method: An inertial viscosity-type variant of Tseng's forward-backward-forward (extragradient) method: an extrapolation (inertial) term is added from the two previous iterates, a single metric projection produces the half-step, a forward correction using the operator difference gives the next iterate, and a viscosity contraction anchors the sequence to force strong convergence. The step size is chosen by a self-adaptive rule using consecutive iterate and operator values, so the Lipschitz constant is not needed.
contribution: A strong-convergence theorem for the inertial viscosity Tseng scheme applied to pseudomonotone variational inequalities, requiring only one projection per iteration and no prior Lipschitz constant, together with computational comparisons against existing extragradient variants and an application to variational inequalities from optimal control.

mathematical_objects.name: Variational inequality problem
mathematical_objects.role: The problem being solved; its solution set is the fixed target of the iteration and the object whose existence and attainment the convergence theorem concerns.

mathematical_objects.name: Pseudomonotone operator
mathematical_objects.role: The monotonicity assumption on the governing map; weaker than monotone, it is the structural condition under which the scheme is proved to converge and the reason standard projected-gradient iterations fail.

mathematical_objects.name: Tseng's forward-backward-forward method
mathematical_objects.role: The base iteration being modified; its forward correction step is what lets the method use a single projection instead of the two required by the Korpelevich extragradient method.

mathematical_objects.name: Inertial extrapolation
mathematical_objects.role: Adds a multiple of the previous step to the current point to accelerate the iteration; its interaction with the projection and correction steps is part of what the convergence proof must control.

mathematical_objects.name: Viscosity approximation
mathematical_objects.role: Contraction-anchored regularization that upgrades weak convergence (typical for extragradient methods on pseudomonotone problems) to strong convergence.

mathematical_objects.name: Metric projection
mathematical_objects.role: The single feasibility-restoring operation per iteration; reducing its use from two evaluations to one is the stated computational advantage.

mathematical_objects.name: Self-adaptive step size
mathematical_objects.role: Sets the step from observed iterate and operator increments so the algorithm runs without knowledge of the Lipschitz constant.

limitations: Only abstract and introduction were extracted; the Preliminaries, Main results and Numerical examples sections were not available, so the exact step-size formula, the precise assumption set of the convergence theorem, and any rate statement could not be verified from the source. Card written at low confidence per curator protocol.
Abstract claims improvement over known results and reliability from 'several computational tests'; generality of that benchmark comparison cannot be assessed from the extracted text.

Strong convergence for pseudomonotone VIs here rests on sequential weak continuity of the operator, an assumption that excludes some operators of interest; the extracted text states it as a definition but the theorem's full hypothesis list was not visible.
No complexity or iteration-count guarantee is stated in the available text, only asymptotic convergence.
open_questions: What is the convergence rate (e.g. non-asymptotic or ergodic) of the inertial viscosity Tseng scheme under pseudomonotonicity?
How large can the inertial parameter be taken while preserving strong convergence, and how does it trade off against the viscosity contraction factor?
Does the self-adaptive step-size rule remain valid when the operator is only locally Lipschitz?
cross_domain_note: General optimization / monotone operator theory; no biological content. Clears the charter routing test trivially. Variational-inequality solvers of this type are used in equilibrium modelling and inverse problems that computational biology work draws on.

title: On the completeness of several fortification-interdiction games in the Polynomial Hierarchy
problem: Tri-level fortification-interdiction games (a defender fortifies, an attacker interdicts, a user then operates the infrastructure) are solved in the literature by ad hoc decomposition methods, but their exact position in the polynomial hierarchy is largely unknown. Where do the standard fortification problems sit, and can that be pinned down even in the commonly used unit-cost regime?
setting: Discrete tri-level (and multi-level) combinatorial optimization: knapsack, max-flow, shortest-path, critical-node, and an electric-grid defence problem, each in a Defender-Attacker-Defender form. Emphasis on the unit fortification / unit attack weight case, where budget constraints become cardinality constraints. Worst-case computational complexity, no probabilistic or average-case component.
method: Polynomial-time many-one reductions from canonical quantified problems (quantified Boolean / quantified combinatorial problems complete for Sigma^p_2 and Sigma^p_3, and generalized quantified knapsack for arbitrary levels) to each fortification problem, matched with membership arguments placing the problem in the same class. A multi-round interdiction knapsack with arbitrary lower-level weights and profits is used as a structural gadget to lift completeness to any level of the hierarchy.
contribution: Establishes Sigma^p_2-completeness of the max-flow interdiction with fortification, the shortest-path interdiction with fortification, and an electric-grid fortification problem (unit fortification costs); Sigma^p_3-completeness of the multi-level critical-node problem with unit weights and profits, refining a prior tree-case result; and completeness for every level of the polynomial hierarchy of the multi-round interdiction knapsack with unit fortification and attack costs, giving a reusable base problem for future hardness proofs of protection-interdiction games.

mathematical_objects.name: Polynomial hierarchy
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity scale on which every result is stated; the paper locates each fortification problem at a specific level and, for the multi-round knapsack, at every level simultaneously.

mathematical_objects.name: Many-one reduction
mathematical_objects.role: The proof instrument: each hardness claim is a polynomial reduction from a known complete problem for the target class into the fortification problem.

mathematical_objects.name: Multilevel / tri-level optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The problem structure under study; the nesting of min/max quantifiers over successive players is exactly what forces the problems above NP.

mathematical_objects.name: Network interdiction problem
mathematical_objects.role: The inner two levels (attacker plus user) for the graph-based instances; their polynomial or NP-hard lower level determines the base level from which fortification adds one quantifier.

mathematical_objects.name: Fortification
mathematical_objects.role: The outermost decision layer that makes chosen elements immune to attack; adding it is the operation whose complexity cost the paper measures.

mathematical_objects.name: Knapsack problem
mathematical_objects.role: The structure-poor base problem used as a gadget; arbitrary lower-level weights and profits let the reduction be iterated to reach any hierarchy level.

mathematical_objects.name: Critical node problem
mathematical_objects.role: Graph-fragmentation problem whose fortified multi-level version is shown Sigma^p_3-complete even with unit weights, sharpening the known weighted/tree case.

limitations: Results are worst-case hardness classifications; they say nothing about instances met in practice or about the performance of the decomposition algorithms currently used.

Membership arguments are sketched in the extracted text but the full proofs (and the precise quantified base problems) are in sections not extracted; the exact reduction gadgets are not verifiable from abstract/intro/conclusion alone.
Several completeness results are specifically for the unit-cost regime; the conclusion notes the general-cost SPIPF and TEPGFP cases remain open.
For the multi-level knapsack the 'any level' result needs an arbitrary number of fortification-interdiction rounds; with a fixed small number of rounds the picture is only partly resolved.
open_questions: Is there a special structure on the lowest-level knapsack weights/profits that lowers complexity without collapsing the problem to P?
What is the complexity of the multi-level critical-node problem with unit weights on structured graph classes such as trees, where the lower level is polynomial?
Can the SPIPF and the electric-grid fortification problem be classified when both fortification and attack costs are arbitrary?
cross_domain_note: Pure computational-complexity / combinatorial-optimization methodology; no biology. The DAD framework and the hierarchy-completeness technique transfer to any infrastructure-protection or robust discrete-optimization setting.

title: On Some Versions of Subspace Optimization Methods with Inexact Gradient Information
problem: Accelerated first-order methods are complexity-optimal for convex smooth minimization, but many settings provide only an inexact gradient, and standard accelerated schemes accumulate that inexactness in their convergence bounds. Can subspace-optimization methods, which are known not to accumulate gradient error, be given a full complexity account that also charges for solving their low-dimensional subproblems, and can they be extended beyond convexity?
setting: Convex smooth minimization with an L-Lipschitz gradient, and its relaxation to gamma-quasar-convex (weakly quasi-convex) functions satisfying a quadratic-growth / Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. The gradient is available only with bounded additive noise of level delta_1; the inner subspace subproblems are solved inexactly to a controlled function-value accuracy. Deterministic analysis; numerical experiments including a non-convex quasar-convex problem.
method: Modifications of two subspace-optimization schemes: Nemirovski's conjugate gradient method and Sequential Subspace Optimization (SESOP), each run with an inexact gradient. The inner low-dimensional subproblems are solved by the ellipsoid method or by a multidimensional dichotomy, and the subproblem accuracy is linked explicitly to the inexactness conditions so the total number of (full-dimensional) gradient evaluations, outer plus inner, can be bounded. A restart scheme and a stopping rule handle the quasar-convex case.
contribution: Linear convergence of the restarted conjugate gradient method with additive gradient noise for quasar-convex functions under quadratic growth, with a stopping rule trading solution quality against iteration count; a total gradient-call complexity for SESOP and CG when the subproblems are convex, showing the inner solves (ellipsoid / dichotomy) do not materially inflate cost and the schemes stay first-order; and confirmation that neither method accumulates the gradient inexactness, converging to an O(delta_1^2/mu) noise floor.

mathematical_objects.name: First-order method
mathematical_objects.role: The class of algorithms studied and the cost model: complexity is measured in full-dimensional gradient evaluations, and the paper insists its modified schemes remain within this class despite the inner solves.

mathematical_objects.name: Inexact gradient oracle
mathematical_objects.role: The perturbation model; the central question is whether its effect accumulates across iterations, and the answer (it does not, for these methods) is the main qualitative result.

mathematical_objects.name: Subspace optimization
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithmic idea under analysis: minimize the objective over a sequence of low-dimensional affine subspaces spanned by gradients and previous steps.

mathematical_objects.name: Conjugate gradient method
mathematical_objects.role: The second subspace method treated; its convergence proof is generalized to inexact gradients and to the quasar-convex setting with restarts.

mathematical_objects.name: Quasar-convexity
mathematical_objects.role: The non-convex relaxation under which the linear-convergence result is established; the parameter gamma appears directly in the achievable accuracy.

mathematical_objects.name: Quadratic growth condition
mathematical_objects.role: The error-bound-type regularity that, combined with quasar-convexity and restarts, yields linear rather than sublinear convergence.

mathematical_objects.name: Ellipsoid method
mathematical_objects.role: The subroutine for the inner low-dimensional subproblems; its known complexity is what makes the total gradient-call count computable when subproblems are convex.

mathematical_objects.name: Accelerated gradient method
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity benchmark: the paper contrasts its non-accumulating error behavior with accelerated methods that do accumulate inexactness.

limitations: The conjugate-gradient linear-convergence result requires the inexact gradient norm to be sufficiently large at each iteration; the stopping rule is a workaround, not a removal of the assumption.
The total-complexity bound for the inner solves assumes the subspace subproblems are convex; the non-convex subproblem case is not covered.
Solution quality for CG can degrade to O((1/gamma) sqrt(epsilon_0/mu) delta_1), a dependence on the initial residual that the extracted text flags but does not fully resolve.
Only additive gradient inexactness is treated; multiplicative or stochastic noise models are outside the analysis.
Empirical support is a small set of experiments (including one non-convex quasar-convex problem); 'fastest of the compared methods' rests on specific conditioning regimes.
open_questions: Can the large-gradient-norm requirement for CG be dropped entirely rather than mitigated by a stopping rule?
What is the total gradient-call complexity when the inner subspace subproblems are themselves non-convex?
Do these non-accumulation guarantees extend to stochastic (rather than adversarial bounded) gradient noise?
cross_domain_note: General convex / non-convex optimization methodology, no biological content. Inexact-gradient first-order methods are directly relevant to large-scale model fitting where exact gradients are unavailable.

title: Approximate Projections onto the Positive Semidefinite Cone Using Randomization
problem: Projecting an n-by-n symmetric matrix onto the positive semidefinite cone is a core subroutine (in SDP solvers, correlation-matrix repair, Lyapunov solutions), but the exact projection needs a full eigendecomposition at O(n^3) cost, which is intractable for large n. Can an accurate approximate projection be computed in sub-cubic time with a usable error guarantee?
setting: Real symmetric matrices, Frobenius-norm projection onto the PSD cone. The working assumption is that the matrices of interest have rapidly decaying singular values so a low-rank surrogate has small truncation error. A user-chosen rank parameter k << n controls an accuracy/speed trade-off. Analysis gives probabilistic (not worst-case deterministic) error bounds; experiments on matrices up to n ~ 20,000.
method: Two randomized numerical linear algebra algorithms. The first draws a random sketch of the matrix, forms a low-rank approximation, and applies an exact eigendecomposition to the resulting small matrix, then reconstitutes the projection. The second first rescales the matrix so that the leading singular values line up with the largest positive eigenvalues, biasing the sketch toward the subspace that survives PSD projection and away from large negative eigenvalues that are zeroed anyway. Both cost O(k n^2) and use a single pass.
contribution: A randomized approximate PSD projection at O(k n^2) instead of O(n^3), in one pass over the matrix (unlike Krylov-based approximations that need multiple passes and suffer finite-precision instability); a scaling variant that improves accuracy by aligning the sketch with positive eigenspace; and probabilistic error bounds showing the error decreases as the sketch rank k grows, with large-scale numerical validation.

mathematical_objects.name: Projection onto the positive semidefinite cone
mathematical_objects.role: The operation being approximated; its exact closed form (eigendecompose, zero negative eigenvalues, recombine) is the O(n^3) baseline the paper replaces.

mathematical_objects.name: Randomized numerical linear algebra
mathematical_objects.role: The framework supplying the sub-cubic low-rank approximation; a random sketch collapses the matrix to a small one before any eigen-work is done.

mathematical_objects.name: Low-rank matrix approximation
mathematical_objects.role: The surrogate on which the projection is actually computed; its truncation error, small when singular values decay, is the dominant source of approximation error.

mathematical_objects.name: Eigendecomposition
mathematical_objects.role: Applied exactly but only to the reduced k-by-k (or k-column) matrix; moving it off the full matrix is what buys the speedup.

mathematical_objects.name: Frobenius norm
mathematical_objects.role: Defines the projection (minimizer of ||X - Y|| over PSD Y) and is the norm in which the probabilistic error bounds are stated.

mathematical_objects.name: Probabilistic error bound
mathematical_objects.role: The theoretical deliverable: bounds the projection error as a function of the sketch rank k, replacing the deterministic guarantee of the exact method.

mathematical_objects.name: Spectral scaling / preconditioning
mathematical_objects.role: The second algorithm's device: rescale so leading singular values match the largest positive eigenvalues, concentrating the random sketch on the subspace relevant after projection.

mathematical_objects.name: Positive semidefinite cone
mathematical_objects.role: The convex constraint set; its self-dual spectral structure is what gives the projection a closed form and lets a low-rank sketch approximate it well.

limitations: The method is only accurate when the input matrix is well approximated by a low-rank matrix (fast singular-value decay); for matrices with flat spectra the O(k n^2) approximation can be poor and the paper does not characterize that failure regime quantitatively in the extracted text.
Error bounds are probabilistic and stated in the Frobenius norm; the constants and failure probabilities, and how tight the bounds are in practice, are in sections not extracted.
The paper studies the projection subroutine in isolation and explicitly does not analyze end-to-end convergence or accuracy when the approximate projection is dropped into a first-order SDP solver.
The scaling variant only 'in some cases' improves the approximation; when it helps versus hurts is left empirical.
Choice of the rank parameter k is left to the user with no adaptive rule; adaptive rank-revealing versions are named only as future work.
open_questions: How does using the approximate projection inside a first-order SDP solver affect that solver's overall convergence and final accuracy?
Can the rank k be chosen adaptively from the observed spectrum rather than fixed a priori?
For which matrix classes does the positive-eigenvalue scaling reliably beat the plain randomized sketch?
cross_domain_note: Numerical linear algebra / matrix algorithms methodology; no biology. PSD projection is a subroutine in covariance/correlation-matrix estimation and kernel methods used in computational biology, but nothing here depends on that.

title: Properties of Turnpike Functions for Discounted Finite Markov Decision Processes
problem: For a discounted finite Markov decision process, value iteration eventually starts producing only optimal policies after some number of iterations, the turnpike integer. As a function of the discount factor this turnpike function governs the true complexity of value iteration, yet its structure (continuity, boundedness, piecewise behavior) near the discount factors where the optimal policy set changes is only partly understood. What are its properties, and can the problematic discount factors be detected efficiently?
setting: Discrete-time MDPs with finite state and action sets, infinite-horizon expected total discounted reward, discount factor alpha in [0,1). Terminal rewards are not assumed zero (a generalization over prior work). Analysis is exact and combinatorial; complexity is measured as strongly polynomial (arithmetic-operation count independent of the magnitude of the data).
method: Classify discount factors as regular or irregular (break points and touching points) via comparisons of finite-step transition probabilities between deterministic policies, which can be done in strongly polynomial time. On intervals free of irregular points, analyze the turnpike function using the analyticity of value functions there, proving upper semicontinuity and a boundedness/finite-partition equivalence. For small discount factors, bound the turnpike function by the number of states and build a value-iteration-based strongly polynomial solver valid for all sufficiently small alpha.
contribution: A strongly polynomial algorithm to test whether a discount factor is irregular; a proof that the turnpike function is upper semicontinuous on each partition interval and that an interval splits into finitely many constant (turnpike) subintervals if and only if the turnpike function is bounded there; sufficient conditions for boundedness near irregular points (with a counterexample showing the known necessary conditions are not sufficient); and a proof that for small discount factors the turnpike function is bounded by the number of states, giving a strongly polynomial value-iteration solver for all small discount factors.

mathematical_objects.name: Markov decision process
mathematical_objects.role: The object being solved; finiteness of state and action sets is the standing assumption under which every result holds.

mathematical_objects.name: Value iteration algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm whose convergence time is the subject; the turnpike function is precisely the iteration count past which it emits only optimal policies.

mathematical_objects.name: Turnpike function
mathematical_objects.role: The central object: the map from discount factor to the number of value iterations needed before all generated policies are optimal.

mathematical_objects.name: Discount factor
mathematical_objects.role: The parameter over which the turnpike function is studied; its classification into regular and irregular points organizes the whole analysis.

mathematical_objects.name: Strongly polynomial algorithm
mathematical_objects.role: The complexity standard for the detection algorithm and the small-discount solver; contrasts with value iteration, which is only weakly polynomial.

mathematical_objects.name: Blackwell optimality
mathematical_objects.role: Characterizes optimal policies for discount factors near 1 (above the largest break point); invoked in framing the open problem of solving for all alpha.

mathematical_objects.name: Upper semicontinuity
mathematical_objects.role: The regularity proved for the turnpike function on irregular-point-free intervals; the piecewise-constant structure is what makes turnpike intervals well defined.

mathematical_objects.name: Optimal policy set
mathematical_objects.role: Constant on each partition interval; irregular points are exactly where it changes, which is why the turnpike function can jump there.

limitations: Everything depends on finiteness of both state and action sets; the conclusion states that for infinite state or action sets optimal policies may not exist and the turnpike integer can be infinite, so the theory does not extend as stated.
The sufficient conditions for boundedness near an irregular point are not shown to be necessary; a full characterization of boundedness is not obtained.

The strongly polynomial solver is proved only for 'small' discount factors below an explicit threshold; solving efficiently for discount factors in an arbitrary interval, or near 1, is left as an open direction.
Proofs and the exact algorithm statements are in sections not extracted; the card relies on the abstract, introduction and conclusion summaries.
open_questions: Can one design an algorithm that returns a policy optimal for all discount factors in a left and right neighborhood of a given alpha, by locating the endpoints of its partition interval?
Are there checkable necessary-and-sufficient conditions for the turnpike function to be bounded near an irregular point?
Can the break points be computed efficiently, enabling parametric dynamic programming across all discount factors?
cross_domain_note: General algorithmic / dynamic-programming complexity theory; no biological content. MDP solution methods are part of the reinforcement-learning toolkit that computational biology (e.g. sequential experimental design) draws on.

title: Error Bound Analysis for the Regularized Loss of Deep Linear Neural Networks
problem: The regularized squared loss of a deep linear network is non-convex with a hierarchical product structure, and existing convergence analyses of gradient descent are tied to specific initializations and only cover convergence to global minima. Can the local geometry around every critical point (global min, local min, or saddle) be characterized well enough to conclude linear convergence of first-order methods regardless of which critical point is approached?
setting: Objective is ||W_L ... W_1 - Y||_F^2 plus a sum of Frobenius-norm penalties lambda_l ||W_l||_F^2, with L >= 2 layers, arbitrary target matrix Y, and each hidden width at least as large as the input and output widths (an explicit assumption). Mild conditions on the regularization parameters. Deterministic full-batch analysis of local geometry; numerical experiments with gradient descent.
method: Specialize an existing closed-form characterization of the critical-point set of the regularized deep linear loss under the width assumption, obtaining an explicit description of that set. Then prove that near every critical point the distance to the critical-point set is bounded by a constant times the gradient norm (a local error bound / Lojasiewicz-type inequality with exponent 1/2). Feed this into the standard error-bound-implies-linear-convergence framework for smooth non-convex problems.
contribution: A closed-form characterization of the critical-point set of the regularized deep linear loss for networks of arbitrary depth (previous results covered two layers and only global minima), and a proof that this loss satisfies a local error bound at every critical point under mild width and regularization conditions. The error bound quantifies distance to the critical set by the current gradient norm and hence implies linear convergence of gradient descent to a critical point, matched by experiments.

mathematical_objects.name: Deep linear network
mathematical_objects.role: The model whose loss landscape is analyzed; the product W_L...W_1 is the source of non-convexity and the hierarchical structure the analysis must handle.

mathematical_objects.name: Regularized squared loss
mathematical_objects.role: The specific objective; adding the Frobenius penalties is what makes existing unregularized-network analyses inapplicable and what the paper's geometry is about.

mathematical_objects.name: Error bound condition
mathematical_objects.role: The regularity property proved: distance to the critical set is controlled by the gradient norm; it is the hinge from which linear convergence follows.

mathematical_objects.name: Critical point set
mathematical_objects.role: The target set for the error bound; the paper first derives its closed form, then measures approach to it. Includes saddles and local minima, not just global.

mathematical_objects.name: Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality
mathematical_objects.role: Cited as equivalent to the error bound under mild conditions and as the more familiar route to linear convergence of gradient descent on non-convex losses.

mathematical_objects.name: Gradient descent
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm whose linear convergence to a critical point is the payoff of the error bound and is verified numerically.

mathematical_objects.name: Balancedness / approximate balancedness of weights
mathematical_objects.role: Structural condition on layerwise weights used in prior deep-linear analyses; the extracted text positions this work as avoiding the carefully-designed initialization those analyses need.

limitations: No conclusion section was extracted; the exact statement of the error bound (the constant kappa, the neighborhood radius epsilon, the precise 'mild conditions' on widths and regularization) could not be verified from the source. Card at low confidence per curator protocol.
Linearity of the network is essential; the analysis does not extend to nonlinear activations, and the extracted text does not claim it does.
The result guarantees linear convergence to some critical point, which may be a saddle or a poor local minimum; it says nothing about which critical point GD reaches or about solution quality.
Requires every hidden layer to be at least as wide as the input and output layers; bottleneck architectures are excluded.
Empirical validation is limited to demonstrating linear convergence of GD on the regularized loss, not comparison against alternative analyses or optimizers.
open_questions: What is the explicit dependence of the error-bound constant on depth L, the widths, and the regularization parameters lambda_l?
Can an analogous error bound be established for deep networks with nonlinear activations, even locally?
Does the error bound combine with a saddle-escaping argument to guarantee convergence specifically to a local (or global) minimum?
cross_domain_note: Learning theory / optimization landscape analysis; no biological content. Deep linear networks are a standard theoretical proxy for understanding training dynamics of the nonlinear networks used across computational biology.

title: A Distributed Asynchronous Generalized Momentum Algorithm Without Delay Bounds
problem: Asynchronous distributed optimization algorithms usually need a known bound on communication and computation delays to prove convergence, but such a bound is often unavailable or unknown in practice. Can a momentum-accelerated distributed algorithm be designed to converge under totally asynchronous operation, with arbitrarily long (but finite) delays, while retaining fast convergence?
setting: Large-scale convex optimization solved by multiple processors, each updating a block of coordinates and communicating iterates. Totally asynchronous model: arbitrary finite delays between successive computations, between computing and sending, and between sending and receiving. The objective's Hessian is assumed to satisfy a diagonal-dominance condition (known to be necessary for convergence under total asynchrony). Deterministic analysis; simulations on 20-newsgroups text classification.
method: A distributed generalized momentum (GM) update that subsumes heavy ball and Nesterov accelerated gradient as parameter choices. Because the GM update is not itself a max-norm contraction, the analysis composes it with itself: the two-step GM map is shown to be an infinity-norm contraction, and the classical asynchronous-convergence theory for contraction mappings (Bertsekas-Tsitsiklis) is then applied to the two-step algorithm. Parameter conditions are derived for asymptotic convergence and for a linear rate.
contribution: A distributed momentum algorithm that provably converges under total asynchrony with no delay bound, generalizing heavy ball and Nesterov; explicit parameter conditions for asymptotic convergence; a linear convergence rate expressed in the number of computation-and-communication cycles processors complete, with a characterization of how many operations are needed to reach a given error ball; and simulations showing 16-36% fewer iterations than gradient descent, heavy ball, and Nesterov under unbounded delays.

mathematical_objects.name: Totally asynchronous computation model
mathematical_objects.role: The execution model the algorithm must tolerate; permitting arbitrarily long finite delays is exactly what distinguishes this work from partially asynchronous methods that assume a delay bound.

mathematical_objects.name: Generalized momentum method
mathematical_objects.role: The algorithm introduced; a parameterized update whose special cases are the classical momentum methods and whose parameters are tuned for asynchronous convergence.

mathematical_objects.name: Heavy ball method
mathematical_objects.role: One special case recovered by the GM parameterization and a simulation baseline.

mathematical_objects.name: Nesterov accelerated gradient
mathematical_objects.role: The other momentum method subsumed by GM and used as a baseline; GM is shown to need fewer iterations under unbounded delays.

mathematical_objects.name: Maximum-norm contraction mapping
mathematical_objects.role: The property that drives the convergence proof; total asynchrony converges for maps that are sup-norm contractions, and the paper shows the two-step GM map (not the one-step map) is one.

mathematical_objects.name: Diagonal dominance of the Hessian
mathematical_objects.role: The structural assumption on the objective; some form of it is known to be necessary for convergence under total asynchrony and it is what lets the two-step map be a contraction.

mathematical_objects.name: Linear convergence rate
mathematical_objects.role: The performance guarantee, stated per completed computation-and-communication cycle rather than per global iteration, matching the asynchronous setting.

limitations: Convergence requires a diagonal-dominance condition on the Hessian; strongly convex objectives without this structure are not covered, and the condition can be restrictive for coupled problems.
The contraction property holds only for the two-step (composed) update, not the natural one-step momentum update; the algorithm as run is the two-step variant.
Delays must be finite (though unbounded); the analysis does not address genuinely lost messages or permanently failed processors.
The rate is stated in operation cycles, which makes cross-method iteration-count comparisons less direct; the 16-36% improvement figures come from simulations on a single dataset and task.
Algorithm parameters are fixed a priori by the derived conditions; the conclusion notes online parameter adaptation is only future work.
open_questions: Can the diagonal-dominance requirement be relaxed while keeping total asynchrony, or replaced by a weaker verifiable condition?
How should the GM parameters be adapted online to accelerate convergence without breaking the contraction property?
Does the two-step contraction trick extend to other non-contractive accelerated updates under total asynchrony?
cross_domain_note: Distributed / parallel optimization methodology; no biological content. Directly relevant to training large models across compute nodes, a setting computational biology increasingly operates in.

title: Re-uploading quantum data: a universal function approximator for quantum inputs
problem: Data re-uploading makes even a single-qubit circuit a universal function approximator for classical inputs by repeatedly encoding features into trainable gates. When the input is a quantum state rather than classical numbers, its "values" are not available to plug into gate parameters. How can quantum data be re-uploaded so that a small circuit still gives a universal approximator of functions of the input state?
setting: Quantum machine learning with quantum inputs: the data is an arbitrary (possibly multi-qubit) density matrix, available as multiple fresh copies. The processing register is a single ancilla qubit; readout is single-qubit measurement. Target functions are bounded continuous functions of the input state. Analysis is an expressivity / approximation-theory argument, not an empirical benchmark.
method: A sequential architecture: the ancilla qubit is entangled with a fresh copy of the input state via a trainable unitary, the input register is then discarded and reset to a new copy, and the ancilla proceeds unmeasured to the next layer. Alternating trainable entangling unitaries with mid-circuit resets realizes a discrete cascade of completely positive trace-preserving maps on the ancilla, structurally a collision model from open-quantum-system dynamics. Universality is shown by constructing polynomial transformations of the input observables and invoking density of polynomials in the continuous functions.
contribution: A quantum-input re-uploading architecture proved to approximate any bounded continuous function of an arbitrary input state using only one ancilla qubit and single-qubit measurements, with qubit count independent of the number of layers (via reset-and-reuse), and an explicit identification of the construction with a collision-model cascade of CPTP maps.

mathematical_objects.name: Universal function approximation
aliases: density of the model class in C(K)
mathematical_objects.role: The property being established for the architecture; the paper's central claim is that the model class is dense in the bounded continuous functions of the input state.

mathematical_objects.name: Data re-uploading
mathematical_objects.role: The design principle extended from classical to quantum inputs; repeated interaction with fresh copies of the state replaces repeated parameter encoding.

mathematical_objects.name: Completely positive trace-preserving map
mathematical_objects.role: Each layer, after discarding the input register, acts on the ancilla as one CPTP map; the whole circuit is a composition of these, which is the object the expressivity analysis works with.

mathematical_objects.name: Collision model
mathematical_objects.role: The structural analogy: ancilla repeatedly colliding with fresh environment copies; it imports intuition and tools from open-system dynamics into the architecture's analysis.

mathematical_objects.name: Partial trace
mathematical_objects.role: The operation that turns each entangling unitary plus reset into a channel on the ancilla alone; it is what keeps the qubit count from growing with depth.

mathematical_objects.name: Mid-circuit measurement and reset
mathematical_objects.role: Refreshes the input register to a new copy between layers; the mechanism behind the layer-count-independent qubit budget.

mathematical_objects.name: Polynomial approximation
aliases: degree-p polynomial functionals of the density matrix
mathematical_objects.role: The proof route: the architecture is shown to realize polynomial functionals of the input state, which are dense in the continuous functions, giving universality.

limitations: The universality proof is confined to a narrow family of ansatz-agnostic operations (alternating single-qubit rotations and controlled unitaries plus specific polynomial constructions); the conclusion states more general operations are 'largely open'.
Universality is an existence/expressivity statement; no sample-complexity, approximation-rate, or number-of-layers bound as a function of target accuracy is given.
Trainability is only discussed heuristically: the small register 'may' mitigate barren plateaus, but no landscape analysis is provided.
Requires many fresh copies of the input state and reliable mid-circuit reset; the copy cost as a function of accuracy is not quantified in the extracted text.
No demonstration that re-uploading beats a tomography-plus-classical-post-processing pipeline on any concrete task; identified as future work.
open_questions: How does approximation accuracy scale with the number of layers and the number of input copies consumed?
How does expressivity change when the signal register has more than one qubit, and does that give more efficient approximations for specific function classes?
Does the small-register architecture actually avoid barren plateaus, under a proper landscape analysis?
cross_domain_note: Learning theory / approximation theory for a quantum-computing model. Charter-fit concern: this is squarely quantum machine learning and the method is specific to quantum inputs and hardware; the transferable content is the universal-approximation property and the CPTP-cascade / collision-model framing. Would still be worth carding with "biology" deleted (it never appears), but it sits at the edge of the domain's optimization/learning core.

title: Gradient descent reliably finds depth- and gate-optimal circuits for generic unitaries
problem: Synthesizing an arbitrary unitary as a quantum circuit from a parameterized gate set is always possible in principle, but finding depth- and gate-minimal circuits is hard. Prior parameter-search approaches report low success even when the circuit ansatz is nominally adequately parameterized, and respond by heavily overparameterizing. Why do those searches fail, and can gradient descent reliably hit the optimal-size circuit without overparameterization?
setting: Generic n-qubit unitaries, which use all parameters and generically need circuits of maximal size (depth Theta(4^n / n) by parameter counting), as opposed to compiled unitaries that have short circuits. Gate set: arbitrary single-qubit unitaries plus CNOT, possibly under restricted (1D chain or star) hardware connectivity. The synthesis is cast as minimizing the distance between target and realized unitary over the continuous gate parameters. Findings are empirical (hundreds of trials), not proven.
method: Fix a circuit "skeleton" of parameterized gates and minimize the target-vs-realized unitary error over the real parameters by gradient descent (GRAPE-style). The key move is a prescription for choosing the skeleton, in particular the CNOT placement, that avoids topologies in which layer symmetries collapse the number of independent parameters and leave the circuit effectively underparameterized. With such skeletons the random combinatorial search over topologies is eliminated.
contribution: An empirical demonstration that gradient descent finds depth-, entangling-gate-, and total-gate-optimal circuits for generic unitaries without overparameterization, even under 1D or star connectivity, once the circuit skeleton is chosen by a simple prescription; and the diagnosis that earlier random-search failures are caused by inadvertently selecting parameter-deficient skeletons whose layer symmetries reduce the effective parameter count.

mathematical_objects.name: Unitary synthesis
mathematical_objects.role: The task: express a target unitary matrix as a hardware-native gate sequence; depth- and gate-optimality of that sequence is what the method targets.

mathematical_objects.name: Non-convex optimization landscape
aliases: loss landscape of the synthesis objective
mathematical_objects.role: The object whose structure explains success and failure: the paper argues the landscape is benign for gradient descent exactly when the skeleton is not parameter-deficient.

mathematical_objects.name: Gradient descent
mathematical_objects.role: The optimizer under study; the claim is that it converges to the global (optimal-size) solution reliably given a good skeleton, replacing random combinatorial search.

mathematical_objects.name: Overparameterization
mathematical_objects.role: The regime prior work relied on for reliable convergence; the paper's point is that it is unnecessary if the skeleton is chosen well.

mathematical_objects.name: Parameter counting
mathematical_objects.role: Fixes the minimal circuit size for a generic unitary (depth Theta(4^n/n)) and defines what "parameter-optimal" and "parameter-deficient" mean.

mathematical_objects.name: Circuit skeleton / ansatz topology
mathematical_objects.role: The discrete choice that determines whether gradient descent succeeds; the paper's prescription selects skeletons whose layers do not share symmetries that shrink the independent-parameter count.

mathematical_objects.name: Hardware connectivity constraints
mathematical_objects.role: Restriction on which two-qubit gates are allowed; the method is shown to still reach optimal-size circuits under these restricted layouts.

limitations: The results are explicitly empirical ('our investigations are empirical'); there is no proof that gradient descent converges, no characterization of the basin of attraction, and no guarantee the prescribed skeleton is always parameter-optimal.
Evidence is trials up to modest qubit counts; scaling behavior of the success rate as n grows large is asserted to remain reliable but not established.

The mechanism (layer symmetries reducing independent parameters) is argued rather than formally characterized; no general criterion is given for when a skeleton is parameter-deficient beyond the specific prescription offered.
Focus is on generic unitaries that need maximal-size circuits; the compiled / structured-unitary case (short circuits) is treated only as contrast, not analyzed.
Only the arbitrary-single-qubit + CNOT gate set is considered; discrete gate sets (Clifford+T) are mentioned only as related context.
open_questions: Can reliable convergence of gradient descent for these prescribed skeletons be proven, and the basin of attraction characterized?
Is there a general, checkable criterion identifying parameter-deficient circuit skeletons a priori?
Does the success rate stay near one as the qubit number grows into the regime where circuit depth Theta(4^n/n) becomes very large?
cross_domain_note: Non-convex optimization / landscape analysis applied to quantum circuit synthesis. Charter-fit is moderate: the transferable content is about when gradient descent reaches a global optimum on an overparameterization-sensitive non-convex problem, which passes the routing test (no biology), but the paper's claims are empirical rather than an established property, so the concordance-worthy content is thinner than the triage score suggests.
